title: Audit and compliance
summary: Query the tamper-evident audit log and understand how writes are hardened.

blocks.text: Every API access and relevant failure can be recorded in an audit log. Only metadata is stored: path, action, actor, timestamp, IP. Secret values are never logged.

items: GET /v1/audit/events with filters: resource_id, actor_id, action, from, to, limit, offset
Each event carries prev_event_id and integrity_hash forming a SHA-256 hash chain
Modifying or deleting any event breaks the chain for every later entry
The app runs as vault_app, which cannot INSERT into audit_events directly

blocks.text: Audit writes go through a SECURITY DEFINER function (insert_audit_event) owned by a privileged role. Even a compromised app connection cannot fabricate events or bypass the hash chain.

steps.text: Set your API key. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys.
Query recent secret reads.
Notice the response includes metadata only, plus prev_event_id and integrity_hash for chain verification. The actor_id shown is an example UUID.
Export an agent UUID from a prior lesson or from the dashboard. If the list is empty, read a secret first (see Foundations), then re-query.
Filter by a single actor to review one agent's activity.
To forward events to your SIEM, register an AuditSink when constructing the TypeScript SDK client. See the @1claw/sdk package documentation for the AuditSink plugin interface.

blocks.text: Verify integrity by walking the chain from the latest event back to the first, where prev_event_id is NULL. Any break flags tampering.
You can now query the audit log by action and actor and explain why the chain plus SECURITY DEFINER insert makes it tamper-evident, which supports SOC 2 controls like CC6 and CC7.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Audit logs are written continuously and read rarely, so their defects surface at the least convenient moment.

items: Retention is shorter than the question. Regulators ask about periods measured in years and default retention is measured in months, which is discovered during the first audit rather than before it.
Nobody has tested completeness. Negative assurance depends on an event necessarily being recorded, and that claim needs evidence rather than confidence.
The log is queried only after incidents. A log nobody reads routinely is a log whose gaps nobody knows about, and the gaps are what an incident will find.

Attribution collapses onto one identity. Every action attributed to "the agent" satisfies retention and answers nothing, which is why identity separation is an audit concern rather than a tidiness one.

blocks.text: Query your audit log for something ordinary once a month. It keeps the retention window honest and surfaces gaps while they are still cheap to fix.

blocks.situation: An auditor asks you to prove that no agent read the secret at prod/db/root during Q3. You have the audit log.
blocks.question: What can you actually demonstrate?

options.text: That no read occurred, by showing the log contains no matching access event.
options.feedback: This is the claim auditors want and the one a log cannot support on its own. Absence of a record proves nothing unless you can also show the log is complete and tamper-evident for the whole period.

options.text: That no read was recorded, and separately that the log is complete for the period, which together support the claim.
options.feedback: Correct, and the distinction matters. The evidence is the conjunction: no matching event, plus assurance that an event would necessarily have been recorded. Stating it that way is what makes the answer defensible rather than merely confident.

options.text: That no agent had a policy granting access, which is stronger than the log.
options.feedback: Useful supporting evidence and worth presenting, but policies change. Showing the current grant says nothing about what was granted in July unless you can also show the policy history.

options.text: Nothing. Audit logs record access, so they cannot evidence its absence.
options.feedback: Too defeatist. Negative assurance from a complete, tamper-evident log is a normal and accepted audit primitive; it just has to be stated with its completeness condition attached.

quiz.question: What is stored in an audit event?
options: The secret value and the metadata
Only metadata such as path, action, actor, and timestamp
The private key hash
Nothing until export
quiz.explanation: Metadata only: path, action, actor, timestamp. If values were logged the audit trail would become a second copy of every secret, in a store with weaker controls and broader read access.

quiz.question: How does the log resist tampering at write time?
options: Writes go through a SECURITY DEFINER function since vault_app cannot INSERT directly
Events are encrypted with the org KEK
It is read-only after 24 hours
Only admins can query it
quiz.explanation: vault_app has direct INSERT revoked, so all writes funnel through the trusted insert_audit_event function that enforces the chain.

quiz.question: What links each event to the previous one?
options: prev_event_id plus a SHA-256 integrity_hash
A Stripe invoice ID
The actor's IP address
A sequential integer ID
quiz.explanation: prev_event_id plus a SHA-256 integrity_hash, which is the hash-chain construction. It does not prevent tampering; it makes tampering detectable, and that is what turns a list of events into evidence.

title: Lab: prove nobody read it
summary: Build a hash-chained audit log, try to answer an auditor's question, then edit and delete entries and watch the chain object.

blocks.text: The audit lesson said that showing no matching event proves nothing on its own, and that negative assurance needs completeness evidence attached. This lab builds the mechanism that supplies it, in about thirty lines.
Each step appends to the same script, so every run reprints the sections before it. The expected output shown under each step is the new part; scroll to the bottom of your terminal to find it.

steps.text: Build a log where each entry commits to the one before it. That single field is what turns a list into evidence.
A normal, intact log.
steps.code:
1 alice    read   app/config     1f60b80d41853f19
  2 deploy   read   app/config     9f6775b6316dd39e
  3 mallory  read   prod/db/root   7db2cf9f81110058
  4 alice    write  app/config     6c8ab733497f6d9c
verify: intact

steps.text: Now be the person who wants entry three to say something else.
steps.code:
cat >> log.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- edit the entry ---")
edited = copy.deepcopy(log); edited[2]["target"] = "app/config"
print("verify:", verify(edited))

print("\n--- delete it instead ---")
deleted = [e for e in copy.deepcopy(log) if e["seq"] != 3]
print("verify:", verify(deleted))
EOF
python3 log.py

steps.text: Both attempts are detected, and for different reasons worth distinguishing.
steps.code:
--- edit the entry ---
verify: ['seq 3: modified after it was written']

--- delete it instead ---
verify: ['gap: expected seq 3, found 4', 'seq 4: prev hash does not match']

steps.text: Now answer the auditor properly. The claim is two statements, not one.
steps.code:
cat >> log.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- the auditor's question ---")
reads = [e for e in log if e["action"] == "read" and e["target"] == "prod/db/root"]
print(f"  matching events:  {len(reads)}")
print(f"  log complete:     {verify(log) or 'chain intact, no gaps'}")
EOF
python3 log.py

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: The two tampering attempts failed differently, and knowing which is which matters during an investigation.

items: Editing an entry breaks that entry's own hash, because the hash covers its contents. You learn exactly which record was altered.
Deleting an entry breaks two things: the sequence has a hole, and the following entry's prev no longer matches. Deletion is louder than modification, which is the opposite of what most people expect.

Neither is prevented. A hash chain is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof, and the distinction is the whole design: you cannot stop someone with write access from changing a file, you can make it impossible to do so quietly.

blocks.text: This is why the answer to "prove nobody read it" is two statements joined together: no event matches, and the log is complete and unmodified for the period. The first alone is worthless, and it is the one people give.

A chain verified only by the party who could tamper with it is weaker than it looks. Real deployments anchor it somewhere the operator does not control: a periodic hash published externally, a write-once store, or a third party countersigning.

Every property this lab demonstrates is one STRIDE calls repudiation. An actor denies having done something and you cannot prove otherwise, which is a security failure with no confidentiality breach, no downtime, and nothing an intrusion detector would ever flag.

quiz.question: Why does deleting an entry produce two errors rather than one?
options: Deleted entries are cached and reappear
Deletion corrupts the file structure
The sequence has a hole and the next entry's prev hash no longer matches
The genesis hash is recomputed
quiz.explanation: Sequence continuity catches the hole and the chain catches the broken link. Deletion is noisier than modification, which surprises most people.

quiz.question: What does a hash chain actually provide?
options: Tamper-evidence: alterations cannot be made quietly
Prevention of unauthorised writes
Tamper-proofing: entries cannot be altered
Encryption of log contents
quiz.explanation: Anyone with write access can still change the file. The chain makes the change detectable, which is a different and achievable goal.

quiz.question: What is the complete answer to 'prove nobody read this secret in Q3'?
options: The access policy did not permit it
No event matches the query
No event matches, and the log is verifiably complete and unmodified for the period
The secret was rotated at the end of Q3
quiz.explanation: Negative assurance is a conjunction. The first statement alone is the one people give and it establishes nothing without the second.

title: Lab: answer a question your log is too young to answer
summary: Set a retention window, then ask about a period that falls outside it and watch an empty result look like an answer.

blocks.text: The audit lab showed how to prove a log is complete and unmodified. This one is about the other half of that claim, which is the period it covers, and it is the half people discover during an audit rather than before one.

steps.text: Set a retention window and ask two questions across it.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/ret.py <<'EOF'
import datetime

RETENTION_DAYS = 90
today  = datetime.date(2026, 9, 7)
cutoff = today - datetime.timedelta(days=RETENTION_DAYS)

events = [{"date": datetime.date(2026, 2, 14), "actor": "mallory", "target": "prod/db/root"},
          {"date": datetime.date(2026, 7,  2), "actor": "deploy",  "target": "app/config"}]
kept = [e for e in events if e["date"] >= cutoff]

print(f"today {today}, retention {RETENTION_DAYS}d, cutoff {cutoff}")
print(f"events still in the log: {len(kept)} of {len(events)}\n")

for label, start, end in [("Q3 (Jul-Sep)", datetime.date(2026,7,1), datetime.date(2026,9,30)),
                          ("Q1 (Jan-Mar)", datetime.date(2026,1,1), datetime.date(2026,3,31))]:
    hits = [e for e in kept if start <= e["date"] <= end and e["target"] == "prod/db/root"]
    covered = start >= cutoff
    print(f"  {label}: {len(hits)} matching event(s)   log covers this period: {covered}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/ret.py

steps.text: Both queries returned zero for prod/db/root. Only one of those zeros means anything.
steps.code:
today 2026-09-07, retention 90d, cutoff 2026-06-09
events still in the log: 1 of 2

  Q3 (Jul-Sep): 0 matching event(s)   log covers this period: True
  Q1 (Jan-Mar): 0 matching event(s)   log covers this period: False

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: There was a read of prod/db/root in February. It is not in the answer because it is not in the log, and a query that returns nothing looks identical whether the event never happened or the record was aged out.

items: Negative assurance needs three things, not two: no matching event, a log that is complete and unmodified, and a retention window that actually covers the period in question.
Default retention is usually months and regulators usually ask about years, which is a mismatch you want to discover before the request rather than during it.
Any query tool should report the window it searched alongside the result. An empty result set with no stated coverage is not an answer.

blocks.text: Check your retention against the longest period anyone could ask about, not against the period you expect to investigate. Incident questions look back weeks; compliance questions look back years.
This is also why exporting the audit log to durable storage matters. Platform retention is an operational setting; your obligation to answer is not, and the two are set by different people.

quiz.question: Both queries returned zero. Why is only one of them informative?
options: Q1 events are archived separately
The Q1 query used the wrong date range
The log does not cover Q1, so zero means no records rather than no events
The Q3 result was cached
quiz.explanation: An empty result looks the same whether nothing happened or nothing was kept. Without stated coverage the zero carries no information.

quiz.question: What does complete negative assurance require?
options: A signed attestation from the provider
No matching event and a tamper-evident log
An access policy showing it was not permitted
No matching event, plus completeness, plus a retention window covering the period
quiz.explanation: The audit lab established the first two. Coverage is the third, and it is the one that fails quietly because it is a setting rather than a property of the data.

quiz.question: Why export the audit log to durable storage?
options: To improve query performance
To reduce storage costs
Platform retention is an operational setting while your obligation to answer is not, and different people set them
Because the platform log is not tamper-evident
quiz.explanation: A retention default chosen for operational convenience has no relationship to the period a regulator will ask about.

title: Agent fleet management
summary: Provision agents at scale, scope their vaults, then rotate a key and deactivate an agent.

blocks.text: When you run dozens or hundreds of agents you need repeatable patterns for enrollment, vault layout, and lifecycle. Bulk provisioning plus tight policies keeps the blast radius small.

items: Shared vault with path-scoped policies: api-keys/** shared, agents/{name}/** per-agent
Per-agent vaults for strict isolation in multi-tenant or compliance setups
Vault binding via vault_ids limits which vaults an agent JWT can touch even if a policy is too broad
Conditional policies add ip_allowlist and time_window on sensitive paths

blocks.text: This lesson uses CLI agent commands. Make sure you completed 'Install the CLI' in Foundations and are logged in with `1claw login`.

steps.text: All steps below use the CLI session from `1claw login`. The TOKEN export is not needed.
steps.code:
# Verify you are logged in:
1claw whoami

steps.text: Bulk provision agents with the CLI. The --scopes flag sets OAuth-style scopes. Fine-grained access is controlled by vault policies (see Agents & Access Control track).
steps.code:
for name in worker-1 worker-2 worker-3; do
  1claw agent create "$name" --scopes "vaults:read"
done

steps.text: List agents and pick one to configure further.
List or create vaults and export their IDs.
steps.code:
1claw vault list
export VAULT_1="first-vault-uuid"
export VAULT_2="second-vault-uuid"

steps.text: Bind each agent to just its intended vaults so a stray policy cannot widen access.
Set transaction guardrails for any agent using the Intents API.

Rotate an agent's API key, which invalidates the old credential. There is no CLI subcommand for this one: `1claw agent keys rotate` rotates a per-chain signing key, which is a different thing. Use the API or the SDK.
steps.code:
# The CLI rotates signing keys, not the agent API key.
# Rotate the API key through the API or SDK:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/rotate-key \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN"

# SDK equivalent:
#   await client.agents.rotateKey(agentId);

steps.text: Deactivate the agent when its task is done. This keeps the audit trail, unlike delete.

blocks.text: Prefer deactivate over delete. A deactivated agent cannot exchange tokens or read secrets, but its records and audit events are preserved for review.
You now rotate a key and deactivate an agent while keeping its audit trail, and you can scope a fleet with vault binding and conditional policies.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Fleets fail by accumulation. No single agent is a problem and the set becomes one.

items: Agents are created and never retired. Deactivation preserves the audit trail where deletion does not, and the absence of a retirement step leaves a growing population of live identities nobody owns.
Policies drift between agents that should match. Three agents doing the same job diverge one exception at a time, and the widest one becomes the effective posture.
Blocked events are unmonitored. Denials are the cheapest signal available precisely because nothing breaks when they fire, and they indicate either a broken client or a steered agent.
Environment tags are set but not enforced. Tagging without env.enforce_agent_environment_scope is documentation, not a control.

blocks.text: Run a quarterly review that lists every agent, its owner, its last activity and its effective scope. Anything with no owner or no recent activity should be deactivated by default.

blocks.situation: Across a fleet of forty agents you see a steady trickle of agent.delegation.blocked events from one agent, roughly twice a day for a week. Nothing has failed and no alert fired.
blocks.question: How do you read this?

options.text: Normal noise. Blocked events mean the controls are working, which is the expected state.
options.feedback: The control is working, and that is exactly why this is worth reading rather than dismissing. A denial is evidence that something repeatedly attempts what it is not permitted to do.

options.text: A misconfigured client retrying a call it was never authorized to make, or an agent being steered toward one. Either way it needs investigating.
options.feedback: Correct. A blocked event is the signal to alert on precisely because nothing breaks when it fires. Persistent, patterned denials are either a bug worth fixing or an injection worth catching, and both are cheaper to find now.

options.text: Rate limiting kicking in; raise max_daily_delegations to clear it.
options.feedback: Raising a limit to stop a warning is how controls get widened for the wrong reason. Rate limiting also emits its own signal rather than a blocked-delegation event.

options.text: Clock skew causing expired delegations to be rejected intermittently.
options.feedback: Expiry rejections do occur, but they would resolve permanently once expired rather than recurring twice a day for a week.

quiz.question: What does vault binding (vault_ids) add on top of policies?
options: It grants access to every vault
It rotates keys nightly
It restricts which vaults the agent JWT works for regardless of policies
It disables audit logging
quiz.explanation: Vault binding is a second layer: even a too-broad policy cannot let the JWT reach vaults outside vault_ids.

quiz.question: Why deactivate an agent instead of deleting it?
options: Deactivate preserves the records and audit trail
Delete keeps the token valid
Deactivate is faster to type
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: Deactivating with --active false blocks access but preserves records and audit events; delete removes them.

quiz.question: For a common set of secrets shared by all fleet agents, what layout is recommended?
options: A single wildcard policy on production
One vault per secret
A shared vault with path-scoped policies
No policies at all
quiz.explanation: One shared vault with path-scoped policies: api-keys/** shared, agents/{name}/** per agent. A vault per agent multiplies the KEKs and the administration without narrowing anything the paths could not.

title: Lab: ask the log who did it
summary: Run the same three actions under one shared identity and under one per job, then ask the log a question an auditor would ask.

blocks.text: The fleet lesson said attribution collapses onto one identity when agents share a credential, and that this satisfies retention while answering nothing. It is a two-line difference in the log and a total difference in what you can say.

steps.text: Build the same activity twice, differing only in who it is attributed to.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/attr.py <<'EOF'
ACTIONS = [("app/key",), ("prod/db/root",), ("app/config",)]

shared = [{"actor": "fleet-agent", "target": t[0]} for t in ACTIONS]
scoped = [{"actor": a, "target": t} for a, t in
          [("agent-search",  "app/key"),
           ("agent-billing", "prod/db/root"),
           ("agent-search",  "app/config")]]

q = "who read prod/db/root?"
for name, log in (("one shared identity", shared),
                  ("one identity per job", scoped)):
    who = {e["actor"] for e in log if e["target"] == "prod/db/root"}
    print(f"{name:22} {q} -> {who}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/attr.py

steps.text: Both logs recorded the read. Only one of them answered the question.
steps.code:
one shared identity    who read prod/db/root? -> {'fleet-agent'}
one identity per job   who read prod/db/root? -> {'agent-billing'}

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: Both logs are complete, tamper-evident and correctly retained. The shared one is also useless for the only question anyone asks during an incident.

items: fleet-agent is a true answer and not an informative one. It names the credential rather than the workload, and during an incident you need to know which workload to stop.
It also removes your ability to scope a response. With one identity you revoke everything or nothing; with several you revoke the one that misbehaved.
And it removes the blocked-event signal, because you can no longer tell which agent is repeatedly attempting something it is not permitted to do.

blocks.text: This is why identity separation is an audit requirement rather than a tidiness preference. A retention policy measured in years, pointed at a log that attributes everything to one actor, satisfies the letter of the requirement and none of its purpose.
The rule of thumb is one identity per workload, not per team, per service or per environment. If two things could ever need to be stopped independently, they need separate identities.

quiz.question: Both logs recorded the read. What did the shared-identity log fail to provide?
options: Retention beyond the policy window
A timestamp
Which workload performed it, which is what you need in order to respond
Tamper evidence
quiz.explanation: The record is true and uninformative. Naming the credential rather than the workload leaves you unable to tell what to stop.

quiz.question: What else does a shared identity take away?
options: Encryption of the audit log
The ability to set policies
Compliance with retention requirements
The ability to revoke narrowly: you revoke everything or nothing
quiz.explanation: Revocation follows identity. One credential across many workloads means any response is all-or-nothing, which turns a contained incident into an outage.

quiz.question: What is the right granularity for agent identities?
options: One per workload, so anything that might need stopping independently can be
One per team
One per environment
One per vault
quiz.explanation: The test is whether two things could ever need to be stopped or investigated separately. If so, they need separate identities.

title: Platform API multitenancy
summary: Register a platform app and bootstrap a user's vault, agent, and signing keys from a template.

blocks.text: The Platform API lets you build multi-tenant products on 1Claw. You register an app, define a bootstrap template, provision users, and hand each user a claim URL, all without your platform being able to read their secrets.
The Platform API requires a Pro or higher plan. Save the returned plt_ key when you create the app; it is not shown again.

items: Templates create a vault, agents, and policies in one atomic operation
In templates use nested intents: { enabled: true }, not the flat intents_api_enabled
signing_keys in the template are provisioned server-side; the plt_ key cannot read them across the org boundary
Bootstrap returns claim_url plus a one-time agent_api_key in summary

steps.text: Exchange your API key for a user JWT. Replace 1ck_your_key_here with your real key.
steps.code:
export ONECLAW_API_KEY="1ck_your_key_here"
export USER_JWT=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/api-key-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"api_key\":\"$ONECLAW_API_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Register a platform app with your user JWT. Silent auth skips the interactive consent screen; use 'interactive' if your platform requires explicit user approval.
steps.code:
curl -X POST "https://api.1claw.co/v1/platform/apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "name": "My DeFi Platform", "slug": "my-defi", "auth_mode": "silent" }'

steps.text: Save the plt_ key now: it is shown only once. Use $PLT_KEY as Bearer in later steps.
steps.code:
# Save from the response:
export APP_ID="paste-app-id-from-response"
export PLT_KEY="paste-plt-key-from-response"

steps.text: Create a bootstrap template. Note intents is a nested object here.
Save the template ID from the response.
Upsert a user.
Save the connection_id from the upsert response.
Bootstrap the user from the template. The response has claim_url and a one-time summary.agent_api_key.
Share the claim_url with the user. It expires in 10 minutes; reissue with the reissue-claim endpoint if it lapses.

blocks.text: For Sign in with 1Claw, the OAuth client_id must be your app slug (for example my-defi), not the app UUID. Passing the UUID returns Unknown client_id.
You now register a platform app and bootstrap a user with a vault, an intents-enabled agent, and server-side signing keys your platform cannot read, plus a claim URL to hand off.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Multi-tenancy failures are rarely subtle and almost always consequential, because the blast radius is every customer at once.

items: platform_locked is omitted at provisioning. It is far easier to set at creation than to retrofit once support workflows have grown to depend on operator reads.
The plt_ key reaches client code. It is a platform-wide credential; anywhere it appears in a browser bundle it is published to every visitor.
Bootstrap runs without an idempotency key. Retries then double-provision, and the second set of resources is attributed to the same connection.
Delegation scopes are set broadly during development. secrets:read added for debugging tends to stay, and it applies across every connected user rather than one.
Claim tokens are treated as durable links. They are one-time and expiring, so a token pasted into a ticket for later is a support case waiting to happen.

blocks.text: Design support tooling around metadata, audit trails and error detail rather than values. Almost all real debugging needs to know that a secret exists and when it last changed, not what it is.

blocks.situation: You are building a product on the Platform API. Your support team needs to help users debug their integrations, which means seeing the secrets those users store in the vaults you provision for them.
blocks.question: How should you design this?

options.text: Provision vaults without platform_locked so support can read values when a user asks.
options.feedback: This is the design decision that ends careers. Operator access to customer secret values is a standing breach risk and a compliance problem, and 'only when the user asks' is a policy, not a control.

options.text: Keep platform_locked set, and give support metadata, audit trails and error detail instead of values.
options.feedback: Correct. Almost all real debugging needs to know that a secret exists, when it was last rotated, and which call failed with what error. None of that requires the value, and designing for it keeps operator access off the table permanently.

options.text: Allow reads but log every operator access to the audit trail.
options.feedback: Logging makes misuse detectable after the fact, which is worth having, but it does not remove the capability. The stronger design removes the ability rather than recording its use.

options.text: Have users paste the secret into a support ticket when they need help.
options.feedback: Now the secret is in a ticketing system, an inbox and a notification, which is strictly worse than a controlled read and is precisely the sprawl the platform exists to prevent.

quiz.question: In a bootstrap template, how do you enable the Intents API on an agent?
options: intents: { enabled: true } (nested)
intents_api_enabled: true (flat)
enable_intents: 1
scopes: [intents]
quiz.explanation: Templates use the nested intents: { enabled: true }; the flat intents_api_enabled is the direct agent-creation form.

quiz.question: What must client_id be for Sign in with 1Claw?
options: The plt_ key
The app slug
The app UUID
The user email
quiz.explanation: The app slug, not the UUID. Passing the UUID returns Unknown client_id, which reads like a misconfiguration rather than a wrong identifier, so it is worth recognising.

quiz.question: Why can't the platform read a bootstrapped user's signing keys?
options: They are deleted after bootstrap
They are only on testnets
Signing keys are never provisioned
The plt_ key cannot read signing keys across the org boundary
quiz.explanation: Signing keys are provisioned server-side and the plt_ key cannot read them across the org boundary, keeping custody separated.

title: Fleet management at platform scale
summary: One bootstrap template can provision a thousand agents. Manage them as a cohort without any single request becoming the largest privilege change the API can express.

blocks.text: The Agent fleet management lesson earlier in this track covers fleets you built by hand: loops of 1claw agent create, per-agent vault binding, per-agent guardrails. That works at dozens of agents. It stops working once a Platform API template has bootstrapped a thousand end users, because at that scale the template is the only thing left that describes them all, and nothing aggregates how far the live cohort has drifted from it.
Requires: a Platform API app and template from Platform API multitenancy, and a Pro or higher plan. Fleet routes accept your plt_ app key or a user JWT for the org that owns the app.

A fleet is simply every agent one template provisioned. The routes answer the two questions a template alone cannot: how many agents are behind the current version, and how do you move them forward without reviewing each one.

steps.text: Check the fleet's status. version_skew breaks the cohort down by the template version each agent was bootstrapped from; spec_hash tells you whether the current version actually changed anything meaningful, since a version number moves on every edit including ones that changed nothing.
Read what is bulk-patchable off the response, rather than assuming it. The allowlist is narrower than a single-agent PATCH and may narrow further over time.
Dry-run a rollout first. A dry run reports the plan and claims no job, so job_id comes back null and it never blocks the real rollout that follows.
Run the rollout. Agents someone edited outside fleet control are skipped, not overwritten, and named in the response under skipped_drifted.

blocks.text: Every route on this page does what it does a thousand times, and nobody reviews it per agent. That single fact explains every restriction below. A patch that would be unremarkable on one agent, raising a spend limit, turning on transaction signing, is a different kind of act when it lands on an entire cohort in one request. So the fleet surface is deliberately narrower than the per-agent API, not wider.

items: Guardrails (max_transaction_value_usd, daily_spend_limit_usd, and the rest) are never bulk-patchable. Raising a limit across a fleet is a thousand separate decisions that happen to share a form, and each one still routes through the per-agent guardrail approval flow.

Capability flags (intents_api_enabled, execution_intents_enabled) are never bulk-patchable. Turning on transaction signing for a whole cohort in one call is the largest privilege change this API can express.

A field outside the allowlist returns 400 naming the field, and refuses the entire patch rather than applying the acceptable parts. A partially-applied bulk patch across a thousand agents is worse than a rejected one.

Hand edits are skipped, not corrected. An agent changed outside fleet control is left alone and the field is recorded on it as drift, the standing answer to "why is this agent still behind". --force overrides the skip but still cannot carry a guardrail or a capability flag, forced or not.
Only one rollout runs per template at a time. A second returns 409, because two concurrent rollouts would race and leave the cohort split across versions.

blocks.text: The MCP server exposes fleets read-only: platform_get_fleet, platform_list_fleet_agents, and platform_plan_fleet_rollout, which always runs as a dry run regardless of what an agent passes. Bulk-patch and pause have no MCP tool. Changing a thousand agents from one call, with no per-agent review, stays a decision for a human at a terminal.
Pausing a fleet deactivates every agent in the cohort at once. The blast radius is the point: this exists for the moment you need a thousand agents to stop immediately, not for routine maintenance.

blocks.scenario: You are reviewing a proposed fleet-management PR before it ships. It adds a new fleet endpoint that lets a plt_ key raise daily_spend_limit_usd for every agent in a fleet in one call, guarded only by a confirm: true flag in the request body.

tools.name: bulk-set-guardrails (proposed)
tools.description: Raises a guardrail field across every agent a template provisioned, in one request.
tools.rationale: It reaches every agent's spend authority in one call (private-data: it touches financial configuration for every end user's agent at once) and, once raised, that authority can move funds externally without further review (external-comms). A confirm flag is a checkbox, not the per-agent guardrail approval flow every other spend-limit change in this API routes through.

tools.name: fleet rollout --dry-run (existing)
tools.description: Reports what a rollout would change without applying anything.
tools.rationale: A dry run changes nothing and claims no job. It has no capability to raise or spend anything, so it closes none of the three circles regardless of what fields the template contains.

tools.name: fleet bulk-patch on system_prompt (existing)
tools.description: Bulk-patches an allowlisted, non-guardrail field like system_prompt across a fleet.
tools.rationale: The allowlist is deliberately built to exclude guardrails and capability flags. A field like system_prompt changes what an agent is told, not what it is authorized to spend or sign, so this stays outside all three circles by design.

blocks.verdict: Reject the proposed endpoint as designed. A confirm flag is not a substitute for the per-agent guardrail approval flow: it collapses a thousand individual spend-limit decisions into one click by one caller, which is exactly the failure mode the real fleet API was built to refuse. If bulk guardrail changes are genuinely needed, they still belong behind the same approval path each individual agent's guardrail widening already requires, not a fleet-scoped shortcut around it.

quiz.question: Why are guardrails like daily_spend_limit_usd excluded from bulk-patchable fields?
options: Raising a spend limit across a fleet is a thousand separate decisions that happen to share a form, so each one still routes through per-agent approval
Guardrails cannot be changed through the API at all
Guardrails are only readable, never writable
Bulk-patching guardrails requires a separate subscription tier
quiz.explanation: The fleet API is deliberately narrower than the per-agent API for exactly this class of field. A patch that is unremarkable on one agent is a different kind of act at cohort scale.

quiz.question: A rollout finds that three agents in the fleet were manually edited outside fleet control. What happens to those three by default?
options: They are overwritten to match the template
The entire rollout fails
They are skipped and recorded as drifted, left alone unless --force is used
They are automatically deactivated
quiz.explanation: Hand edits are skipped, not corrected. Someone changed them for a reason, and a rollout that silently overwrites a thousand such reasons at once is worse than one that names them as drift.

quiz.question: A field outside bulk_patchable_fields is included in a bulk-patch request across 500 agents. What happens?
options: The valid fields are applied and the invalid one is silently dropped
The whole patch is refused with a 400 naming the offending field
The request succeeds and the field is ignored server-side without a warning
Only the first 100 agents receive the patch
quiz.explanation: A partially-applied bulk patch across hundreds of agents is far worse than a rejected one, so the whole patch refuses rather than applying only the acceptable parts.

quiz.question: What does fleet rollout --dry-run actually do?
options: Applies the rollout to a random 10% sample of the fleet
Runs the rollout but reverts it after 24 hours
Requires the same approval as a real rollout, just logged differently
Reports the plan and changes nothing; job_id comes back null so it never blocks the real rollout
quiz.explanation: A dry run claims no job. Because job_id is null, it never collides with the one-rollout-per-template rule, so you can preview freely before committing.

concepts.note: ASI10: a single overpowered bulk action is a rogue-agent-shaped risk even when a human triggers it
the fleet API is narrower than the per-agent API on purpose

title: Declarative charts: provisioning that refuses more than it does
summary: One YAML file describes a whole swarm. What 1claw apply will not do to reality is more interesting than what it will.

blocks.text: Every provisioning step in this course so far has been imperative: create this vault, then this agent, then this policy, one call at a time. 1claw apply takes a single file describing what you want, vaults, agents, policies, connectors, and reconciles reality toward it. If you have used Terraform or Kubernetes manifests, the shape is familiar. What is worth studying closely is not the YAML, it is the list of things apply is built to refuse.

steps.text: See what a chart would change before it changes anything. This never writes.
Apply it. Names in the chart are the reconcile keys: a second apply finds what the first one made by name, not by position.

blocks.text: Both diff and apply are human-only, POST /v1/org/apply/diff and POST /v1/org/apply, and both are server-side reconciliation, not client logic. A chart provisions agents, vaults and access policies, so an agent that could apply one could grant itself access to a vault it cannot currently read.

items: It never deletes. A resource removed from the chart is left alone; there is no --prune. An apply that silently deletes is an apply nobody runs twice, and tearing down stays explicit and separate.

It skips anything edited outside the chart, naming the field that differs, rather than overwriting it. Someone changed it for a reason, and a reconciler that erases that reason at three in the morning is worse than one that does nothing.

It refuses guardrails outright. Transaction limits, host allowlists and approval policies are not chart fields; a reconciler that wrote them directly would be a way around the guardrail approval flow wearing a deployment tool's clothes.

It does not skip your org's approval gates. Apply calls the same handlers the API routes call, so a resource that needs consensus queues an approval exactly as a dashboard click would, and the rest of the chart still applies around it.
Unknown fields are errors, not warnings. A misspelled field that was silently dropped would report success while doing nothing you asked for, and the field's absence would be the only clue.

blocks.text: Renaming an agent in the chart does not rename the agent. It creates a new one under the new name and leaves the old one running, because apply reconciles by name and a changed name is, to the reconciler, a resource it has never seen before.

The drift detection needs a state file, .1claw/apply-state.json, which apply itself writes and reads. That file is what distinguishes "someone edited this since I last applied" from "this existed before I ever ran": a resource that predates your first apply is not drift, and treating it as such would make apply refuse to manage anything that already existed in your org.

This is the same rule fleet rollouts use for hand-edited agents, applied one layer up: a reconciler's job is to move reality toward the declared state, not to erase whatever a human did in between. The two features share that rule because it is the same failure mode either way, an automated tool overwriting a deliberate manual intervention because a file says otherwise.

blocks.scenario: A teammate proposes a --force flag for 1claw apply that would let a chart overwrite fields changed outside the chart, and a --prune flag that deletes any resource no longer listed, to make onboarding new environments faster.

tools.name: apply --force (proposed)
tools.description: Overwrites hand-edited fields to match the chart, bypassing the drift-skip.
tools.rationale: It reaches every resource the chart describes and overwrites configuration a human changed for a reason, without that human being consulted again. That is a standing capability to silently erase manual interventions across a whole org's agents and policies, not a one-time convenience.

tools.name: apply --prune (proposed)
tools.description: Deletes any resource not currently listed in the chart.
tools.rationale: Deleting a vault, agent or policy because a line was removed from a YAML file (accidentally or otherwise) destroys standing access and any credentials or bindings that depended on it, reachable by anyone who can edit the chart file, not only someone with direct API access.

tools.name: 1claw diff -f chart.yaml (existing)
tools.description: Reports what an apply would change, writing nothing.
tools.rationale: A read with no side effects closes none of the three circles regardless of what the chart describes, because nothing is created, changed, or deleted by running it.

blocks.verdict: Reject both flags as designed, for the same reason the real apply refuses guardrail edits: a deployment tool that can silently overwrite a deliberate manual fix, or delete a resource because a line vanished from a file, is a way around the org's actual controls wearing a convenience feature's clothes. If faster environment teardown is the real need, it belongs behind an explicit, separately-authorized teardown command that names what it is about to remove, not a flag on the tool that is supposed to only ever add and reconcile.

quiz.question: A chart removes an agent that was previously listed. What does the next apply do to that agent?
options: Leaves it alone; there is no --prune
Deletes it immediately
Deactivates it but preserves its audit trail
Queues a deletion approval
quiz.explanation: Apply never deletes. A resource removed from the chart is simply left alone; tearing something down stays a separate, explicit action.

quiz.question: An agent's system_prompt was changed by hand during an incident, outside any chart. What happens on the next apply of a chart that also sets system_prompt?
options: The chart's value silently overwrites the hand edit
The apply fails entirely
The field is skipped and named as changed outside the chart; the hand edit is left alone
Both values are merged into one string
quiz.explanation: Apply distinguishes drift (changed since the last apply) from a fresh resource using its own state file, and skips drifted fields rather than overwriting the reason someone changed them.

quiz.question: Why does 1claw apply refuse to change guardrail fields like tx_max_value directly, even when they're written into the chart?
options: Guardrails cannot be expressed in YAML syntax
Guardrails are read-only in this API version
Charts are limited to five resource types
A reconciler writing guardrails directly would be a way around the guardrail approval flow every other edit to them requires
quiz.explanation: Guardrail edits route through the approval flow specifically because they are privileged changes. A declarative tool that could set them directly would bypass that review entirely.

concepts.note: the same hand-edits-are-skipped rule, one layer up
a tool that can provision access is scoped as tightly as the access itself

title: Sub-organizations
summary: Model departments, subsidiaries, or customers as isolated sub-orgs with delegated permissions and their own wallets.

blocks.text: A single flat organization stops working once you have departments with genuinely separate budgets, or a parent company with subsidiaries. Sub-organizations (v0.47) give you a hierarchy with cryptographic isolation between branches.

items: Each sub-org can inherit billing from the parent or manage its own.
Permissions are granted and revoked explicitly per sub-org.
Sub-orgs can generate their own wallets.
Users are added per sub-org, so access does not leak sideways.

blocks.text: Do not confuse this with the Platform API. Sub-orgs partition your own organization; the Platform API provisions resources for other people's users. If you are building a product on 1Claw, you want the Platform API.

steps.text: Create a sub-org.
Grant it a scoped set of permissions.
Add a user to it.
Generate wallets scoped to the sub-org.
Manage the whole lifecycle from the CLI.
steps.code:
1claw sub-org list
1claw sub-org get $SUBORG_ID
1claw sub-org archive $SUBORG_ID

blocks.text: Deleting a sub-org archives it rather than destroying it, which keeps the audit trail intact for anything that happened inside it.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Hierarchies are created for isolation and then eroded for convenience.

items: Permissions are granted at the parent for expedience. A grant made once at the top to unblock someone dissolves the boundary the hierarchy was created to draw.
Sub-orgs are used for what the Platform API does. Modelling your product's end users as sub-orgs works until you need per-user claim flows and billing, and by then migration is expensive.
Archived sub-orgs are assumed gone. Archiving preserves history deliberately, so anything counting active resources needs to account for them.
Wallet quotas are forgotten. Sub-org wallets count toward the org quota, and a per-sub-org wallet strategy consumes it faster than anyone plans for.

blocks.text: The dividing question is whose users these are. Your own departments are sub-orgs; other people's users are the Platform API. Getting it wrong is recoverable and expensive.

blocks.situation: You are the platform team at a company with three product groups that want separate budgets, separate agents, and no visibility into each other's secrets. A colleague suggests using the Platform API, since it is built for multi-tenancy.
blocks.question: Which model fits?

options.text: Platform API, because isolating tenants is exactly what it does.
options.feedback: It does isolate tenants, but the tenants it models are your product's end users, provisioned on their behalf with plt_ keys and claim flows. Using it for your own internal departments imports a consent and billing model you do not want internally.

options.text: Sub-organizations, which partition your own org with delegated permissions and their own wallets.
options.feedback: Correct. The distinction is whose users these are. Sub-orgs are for dividing your own organization; the Platform API is for provisioning on behalf of other people's users.

options.text: Three separate 1Claw organizations, which guarantees isolation.
options.feedback: It does isolate, and it also gives up central billing, cross-group audit and any shared policy. That is a real option for genuinely separate legal entities, not for three groups in one company.

options.text: One org with naming conventions and careful policies per group.
options.feedback: This is isolation by discipline, which degrades the first time someone writes a broad glob. The hierarchy exists so the boundary is structural rather than conventional.

quiz.question: When should you use sub-organizations rather than the Platform API?
options: When you want a second billing account only
When you need more API keys
When provisioning resources for your product's end users
When partitioning your own org into departments or subsidiaries
quiz.explanation: Sub-orgs partition your own organization. The Platform API is for provisioning on behalf of other people's users: a different problem with a different model.

quiz.question: What happens when you delete a sub-org?
options: It is archived, preserving the audit trail
It is permanently destroyed with all records
Its users are deleted too
It is merged into the parent
quiz.explanation: The DELETE endpoint archives the sub-org so historical activity stays auditable.

title: Lab: audit what 1Claw discloses about itself
summary: Fetch every well-known metadata file 1Claw publishes and apply the audit-and-compliance track's own standards to the vendor this course has been teaching from.

blocks.text: Every lesson in this track has asked you to hold your own systems to a standard: disclose what is needed, log what matters, retain what regulators will ask about. This lab holds 1Claw to that same standard, using only what it publishes about itself.

steps.text: Fetch the AI catalog entry, which is 1Claw's own disclosure of what it operates and how to reach it.
steps.code:
curl -s https://1claw.co/.well-known/ai-catalog.json | python3 -c '
import json, sys
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print("host:   ", d["host"]["displayName"])
print("entries:", [e["type"] for e in d["entries"]])
'

steps.text: A declared host identity and a typed list of everything it discloses: an MCP server card, an A2A agent card, and an OpenAPI spec.
Cross-check that against the OAuth protected-resource metadata, which is a second, independent disclosure of the same API.
steps.code:
curl -s https://1claw.co/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource | python3 -c '
import json, sys
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print("resource:", d.get("resource"))
print("auth servers:", d.get("authorization_servers"))
'

steps.text: Two independently maintained files agreeing on the same issuer is exactly the kind of corroboration an auditor looks for.

blocks.text: Nothing here required 1Claw's cooperation beyond what they already publish for exactly this purpose. That is the point: a vendor whose architecture is verifiable from public metadata is giving you the same thing the audit-and-compliance lesson asked you to give your own auditors.

items: Independent corroboration matters more than a single disclosure. One file claiming an architecture is a statement; two separately-maintained files agreeing on the same issuer is evidence.

This is a smaller version of the same negative-assurance problem from the audit lab. These files tell you what is disclosed, not that nothing is missing, and a vendor's well-known directory is not a complete architecture diagram.

The exercise generalises past 1Claw. Before adopting any vendor into a system you will be audited on, check what they disclose about themselves the same way, unprompted, before you ask them a single question directly.

blocks.text: This is genuinely all public, unauthenticated metadata. If you are evaluating 1Claw, or any vendor, as part of your own compliance posture, checking what they disclose without an account is a five-minute exercise worth doing before the sales call.

Public disclosure is necessarily a summary. It tells you the shape of what exists, not the operational detail an SOC 2 report or a real audit would require. Treat this as a first filter, not a substitute for due diligence.

quiz.question: Why does agreement between two independently maintained files matter more than either one alone?
options: It is required by the OIDC spec
It is a coincidence with no significance
Two separately maintained sources agreeing is corroboration; one source alone is just a claim
It makes the files load faster
quiz.explanation: This is the same logic behind cross-referencing any claim: independent agreement is evidence, while a single assertion is not, however official it looks.

quiz.question: What does this lab's method NOT tell you about a vendor?
options: Whether their operational controls, the things an SOC 2 report covers, actually hold up in practice
Their declared architecture
Their public issuer
Whether their metadata is internally consistent
quiz.explanation: Public disclosure is a first filter, not a substitute for real due diligence. It tells you the vendor is willing to be checked, not that everything underneath has been verified.

quiz.question: Why is this exercise worth running before adopting any vendor, not just 1Claw?
options: It is legally required
Every vendor publishes identical files
It is a five-minute, unauthenticated check that surfaces obvious inconsistencies before you invest in a deeper evaluation
It replaces the need for a security questionnaire
quiz.explanation: The value is proportional to the cost: near-zero effort for a real signal, which makes it a sensible first step rather than a complete audit.

title: Capstone: architect a control plane
summary: The closing exercise. Design the whole system for a hostile brief, and defend the trade-offs you make.

blocks.text: This is the last lesson in the course, and it asks for the thing every previous track was building toward: a complete design, with the compromises stated out loud.

The brief. A healthcare scheduling company runs a fleet of agents that read patient referral emails, look up clinician availability, book appointments, and settle small payments to partner clinics. Referrals arrive from outside the organisation. Regulators require that every access to patient data be attributable to a named principal and retained for seven years. The company has been breached once already, through a contractor's leaked API key.
Design it before reading on. Then compare, and pay attention to the places you and the walkthrough disagree, because several of these have more than one defensible answer.

Start from the threat model, not the product. Referral emails are untrusted content by definition, patient records are the private data, and booking confirmations go back out to the referrer. All three circles are present and none can be removed without destroying the product. That settles the shape of everything else: injection will eventually succeed, so the design has to make success cheap.

items: Identity. One agent per function, never one fleet identity. Referral parsing, scheduling, and settlement are three principals with three audit trails, because the seven-year retention requirement is worthless if every action is attributed to "the agent".

Credentials. No agent holds one. Clinical systems and the payment rail are reached through bindings with vault_ref credentials, so the contractor breach that started all this cannot repeat in the same shape.
Storage. Patient identifiers live in a vault with MPC custody, because a single provider holding complete key material is exactly the concentration a regulator will ask about.
Inference. Referral text goes through Shroud, so PII is scrubbed before it reaches a model provider and never enters a third party's logs.
Authorization. Deny-by-default, scoped per path, with environment tags locked on the production agents so a preview identity can never resolve production data.
Human factor. Settlement above a threshold routes to a person with step-up authentication, and the threshold is set where a human will still read the prompt.

blocks.situation: The clinical team asks for one agent that can do all three jobs, arguing that three agents means three integrations to maintain and the same human owns all of them anyway.
blocks.question: How do you answer?

options.text: Agree. One owner means one identity is a fair simplification, and fewer integrations is a real benefit.
options.feedback: The maintenance argument is genuine and the conclusion still fails. A single identity means the referral-parsing path, which consumes attacker-controlled email, carries the settlement credential too. You would be handing an injected agent the payment rail.

options.text: Refuse on principle. Agents must always be single-purpose.
options.feedback: Right answer, wrong reasoning, and the reasoning is what fails you at the next meeting. A rule stated as principle invites an exception the moment it is inconvenient; state the specific consequence instead.

options.text: Keep them separate, because merging puts the settlement capability on the path that reads untrusted email, and offer to reduce the integration cost another way.
options.feedback: Correct. Name the concrete consequence rather than the principle, and take the maintenance concern seriously, because it is real. Shared bindings and a common runtime template address the cost without merging the identities.

options.text: Merge them but add approval on every settlement.
options.feedback: This puts a human in front of every payment in a system doing small settlements at volume, which produces reflexive approval within days. You would have merged the identities and neutralised the control meant to compensate.

blocks.text: Now the part that separates a design from a diagram: say what you gave up. Every choice above has a cost, and a design that claims otherwise has not been thought through.

items: MPC custody adds operational failure modes. Shares can be lost, and a team without key-handling maturity can lock itself out of patient data permanently.
Routing inference through a TEE proxy adds latency to every referral, and attestation proves which code runs, not that the code is correct.
Three identities mean three sets of policies that can drift apart, and drift is how a preview agent ends up with a production grant.
Deny-by-default guarantees a support burden. Someone is blocked on a Friday afternoon by a rule nobody remembers writing.
Approval thresholds decay. Set too low they get clicked through; set too high they never fire. Either way they need revisiting, and nobody schedules that.

blocks.text: If you cannot name what a control costs, you do not yet understand it well enough to defend it when someone asks to remove it. That conversation always comes.

One last thing the brief tried to hide. Nothing above prevents the breach that already happened: a contractor leaked a key. What the design changes is the consequence. The leaked credential is now short-lived, scoped to one path, attributable to one principal, and useless for reaching the payment rail. That is the whole thesis of this course, stated as an outcome rather than a principle.

quiz.question: Why does the brief's threat model settle the shape of the design before any product decision?
options: Regulators require a threat model first
Referral emails cannot be parsed safely
All three trifecta circles are present and none can be removed, so the design must assume injection succeeds
Healthcare data requires MPC by law
quiz.explanation: When no circle can be removed without destroying the product, prevention stops being the goal and limiting the consequence becomes it. That drives identity, credential handling and approval design.

quiz.question: What is the strongest argument against merging the three agents into one?
options: Three audit trails are required by the regulator
It would exceed the agent quota
It would put the settlement credential on the path that consumes untrusted email
Single-purpose agents are a best practice
quiz.explanation: Naming the concrete consequence is what survives a follow-up meeting. Stating it as a principle invites an exception the first time it is inconvenient.

quiz.question: What does the design actually change about the original contractor breach?
options: It prevents credentials from leaking
It makes the leaked credential short-lived, narrowly scoped, attributable, and useless for reaching payments
It removes the need for contractors to hold credentials
It detects the leak faster
quiz.explanation: No design prevents a person from leaking a credential. The measure of the architecture is what an attacker gets when one inevitably leaks.
